chunks: Muhammad ibn Ja'far Abu al-Abbas, from Ayyub ibn Nuh, from Safwan, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb who said: I heard Abu Basir saying:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a woman whose husband had divorced her contrary to the Sunnah, and we said that they are a private family and no one knows them. So he said: It is not anything (i.e., the divorce is null and void).

key_terms.أَهْلُ بَيْتٍ: Here means a private/secluded household, i.e., a family living away from public view, with no witnesses available
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِشَيْءٍ: It is not anything — a standard jurisprudential formula for nullity and complete legal invalidity
key_terms.لِغَيْرِ السُّنَّةِ: Contrary to the Sunnah — referring to divorces that do not meet the prescribed conditions such as: presence of two just witnesses, the woman being in a state of purity (tuhr) without conjugal relations having occurred during it

ai.seo_question: Is a divorce performed contrary to the Sunnah valid in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Abu Basir narrates that he asked Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) about a divorce performed contrary to the prescribed Sunnah method, noting that the couple was a private household with no witnesses. The Imam ruled that such a divorce is completely invalid — 'it is not anything.' This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that divorce (talaq) must strictly follow the conditions stipulated in the Book and the Sunnah; a divorce performed outside these conditions has no legal effect whatsoever, regardless of the couple's social circumstances.
